1.pericope_label: Then he brought me back the way of the gate of the outward sanctuary which looketh toward the east; and it was shut. Then said the Lord unto me; This gate shall be shut, it shall not be opened, and no man shall enter in by it; because the Lord, the God of Israel, hath entered in by it, therefore it shall be shut. It is for the prince; the prince, he shall sit in it to eat bread before the Lord; he shall enter by the way of the porch of that gate, and shall go out by the way of the same. Then brought he me the way of the north gate before the house: and I looked, and, behold, the glory of the Lord filled the house of the Lord: and I fell upon my face. And the Lord said unto me, Son of man, mark well, and behold with thine eyes, and hear with thine ears all that I say unto thee concerning all the ordinances of the house of the Lord, and all the laws thereof; and mark well the entering in of the house, with every going forth of the sanctuary. And thou shalt say to the rebellious, even to the house of Israel, Thus saith the Lord God; O ye house of Israel, let it suffice you of all your abominations, In that ye have brought into my sanctuary strangers, uncircumcised in heart, and uncircumcised in flesh, to be in my sanctuary, to pollute it, even my house, when ye offer my bread, the fat and the blood, and they have broken my covenant because of all your abominations. And ye have not kept the charge of mine holy things: but ye have set keepers of my charge in my sanctuary for yourselves. Thus saith the Lord God; No stranger, uncircumcised in heart, nor uncircumcised in flesh, shall enter into my sanctuary, of any stranger that is among the children of Israel.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch divide the chapter into three parts and keep to its structure; Ellicott works from the wording, reading the shut gate as the outer gate of the sanctuary, insisting the prince is the David named earlier in the book and that this settles the sacrificial worship of these chapters as symbolic, and distinguishing the foreigners who might lawfully sacrifice from those uncircumcised in heart.

Gill places the prophet in the holy place as distinct from the holy of holies, takes the shut gate for one of the inner court, rejects both the high priest and the civil ruler as candidates for the prince in favour of the Messiah, and reads the strangers spiritually as the unregenerate.

Clarke supplies external detail: the gate opened only on sabbaths and new moons, the fat and blood never went to common use, and some manuscripts refer the abominations to the strangers; he also rejects a devotional argument built on the verse as precarious. Wesley keeps the plain civil sense of the prince, glosses the sanctuary as the courts, and identifies the guide as Christ in the appearance of a man.

Henry reads the second survey as a lesson that the things of God bear looking over again, sees the shut gate as perpetuating the memory of the glory that entered there, and turns the prophet's posture into a maxim that the more we see of God's glory the lower we lie in our own eyes.

debates.question: Which court does the shut eastern gate belong to?

positions.position: The inner court, the prophet having been brought from the altar to the holy place.
The outer court, the phrase meaning the outer gate of the sanctuary and the prophet being led out of the inner court where the altar stood.

debates.question: Who is the prince who eats bread before the Lord in the gate?

positions.position: The Messiah, neither the high priest nor the civil ruler.

The David named earlier in the book, which makes the sacrificial worship of these chapters symbolic; the eating cannot be narrowed to the unbloody offerings, since the prince has no priestly function.
The king in the ordinary civil sense, permitted to sit where others might not, eating the offerer's portion.

debates.question: Whose abominations are charged in the closing censure?

positions.position: The nation's own.
Some manuscripts read their abominations, referring the fault to the admitted strangers.

outliers.claim: Records that the shut gate has been pressed into an argument about the mother of Jesus, allows it is as much to the purpose as others offered for that conclusion, and calls the point precarious, one no man should lay stress on.

Argues that foreigners in Israel were allowed and sometimes required to sacrifice, as the prayer at the first temple's dedication recognised, so that what is condemned is admitting men uncircumcised in heart with no real intention of worshipping.

10.pericope_label: And the Levites that are gone away far from me, when Israel went astray, which went astray away from me after their idols; they shall even bear their iniquity. Yet they shall be ministers in my sanctuary, having charge at the gates of the house, and ministering to the house: they shall slay the burnt offering and the sacrifice for the people, and they shall stand before them to minister unto them. Because they ministered unto them before their idols, and caused the house of Israel to fall into iniquity; therefore have I lifted up mine hand against them, saith the Lord God, and they shall bear their iniquity. And they shall not come near unto me, to do the office of a priest unto me, nor to come near to any of my holy things, in the most holy place: but they shall bear their shame, and their abominations which they have committed. But I will make them keepers of the charge of the house, for all the service thereof, and for all that shall be done therein. But the priests the Levites, the sons of Zadok, that kept the charge of my sanctuary when the children of Israel went astray from me, they shall come near to me to minister unto me, and they shall stand before me to offer unto me the fat and the blood, saith the Lord God: They shall enter into my sanctuary, and they shall come near to my table, to minister unto me, and they shall keep my charge. And it shall come to pass, that when they enter in at the gates of the inner court, they shall be clothed with linen garments; and no wool shall come upon them, whiles they minister in the gates of the inner court, and within. They shall have linen bonnets upon their heads, and shall have linen breeches upon their loins; they shall not gird themselves with any thing that causeth sweat. And when they go forth into the utter court, even into the utter court to the people, they shall put off their garments wherein they ministered, and lay them in the holy chambers, and they shall put on other garments; and they shall not sanctify the people with their garments.

schools.summary: Ellicott dates the Levites' apostasy to the later general decline rather than the northern schism, renders the opening words yea, even to bind the passage to what precedes, takes the sons of Zadok as a description of fidelity rather than a genealogy, and observes that wearing the official dress only on duty is here expressly commanded where the older books only imply it. Keil and Delitzsch keep the sequence of the requirements without comment on the reasons.

Gill turns the degraded Levites into a description of ministers who departed from the principles they professed and made their own reason their guide, keeps the literal descent of Zadok through Eleazar, draws a disciplinary parallel from the ancient practice of admitting fallen ministers only to lay communion, and makes the linen headgear a sign of gravity and purity of doctrine rather than a matter of physical fitness.

Clarke refers the degradation to the northern schism and reads the whole passage of the second temple, and gives natural and comparative reasons for the linen: wool contracts dirt and breeds insects, and whatever is taken from a dead body was anciently counted unclean in religion. Wesley makes the sentence a demotion to the lowest offices, reads the reward of the faithful as a standing rule of God's dealing, and explains the change of clothes by the law that common things touching holy things became consecrated.

Henry pictures a householder taking account of his servants and names the compliances that ruined the Levites, noting that when priests go astray many follow; on the linen he keeps to the reason the text gives, that wool causes sweat, requiring dress both cool for work beside constantly burning altars and clean as a sign of purity of mind, and recalls that sweat came in with sin.

debates.question: When did the apostasy of these Levites happen?

positions.position: At the northern schism, when the new king drew as many priests as he could into his worship; the passage belongs to the second temple.
Not then, for at that crisis these priests stood firm; it was in the later general decline that many fell into idolatry.
In the recorded compliances of priests who bowed in an idol's house or built an altar for a king.

debates.question: Why may the priests wear no wool?

positions.position: For the reason the text gives, that wool causes sweat: they must be cool for work beside burning altars and clean as a sign of purity of mind, sweat itself belonging to the curse.
Because wool contracts dirt and breeds insects, and because it is an animal substance, whatever is taken from a dead body being anciently unclean in religion.
The physical question is left alone; the linen headgear signifies gravity, subjection to God and purity of doctrine.

debates.question: Are the sons of Zadok a lineage or a character?

positions.position: A description: any priest who kept faith in an apostasy is called by the name of the man who stayed loyal in a rebellion where even the high priest went over.
A literal descent, through Eleazar in the line of Phinehas; the name itself means righteous.

outliers.claim: Supports the vegetable-versus-animal reason for linen from outside Israel, that Egyptian priests wore linen with shoes of matting and that Muslims will not write their scripture on skin, counting it a defilement.
Draws a disciplinary parallel from later church practice, that ministers who had sinned foully were formerly not restored to office on repentance but admitted only to lay communion.

20.pericope_label: Neither shall they shave their heads, nor suffer their locks to grow long; they shall only poll their heads. Neither shall any priest drink wine, when they enter into the inner court. Neither shall they take for their wives a widow, nor her that is put away: but they shall take maidens of the seed of the house of Israel, or a widow that had a priest before. And they shall teach my people the difference between the holy and profane, and cause them to discern between the unclean and the clean. And in controversy they shall stand in judgment; and they shall judge it according to my judgments: and they shall keep my laws and my statutes in all mine assemblies; and they shall hallow my sabbaths. And they shall come at no dead person to defile themselves: but for father, or for mother, or for son, or for daughter, for brother, or for sister that hath had no husband, they may defile themselves. And after he is cleansed, they shall reckon unto him seven days. And in the day that he goeth into the sanctuary, unto the inner court, to minister in the sanctuary, he shall offer his sin offering, saith the Lord God. And it shall be unto them for an inheritance: I am their inheritance: and ye shall give them no possession in Israel: I am their possession. They shall eat the meat offering, and the sin offering, and the trespass offering; and every dedicated thing in Israel shall be theirs. And the first of all the firstfruits of all things, and every oblation of all, of every sort of your oblations, shall be the priest’s: ye shall also give unto the priest the first of your dough, that he may cause the blessing to rest in thine house. The priests shall not eat of any thing that is dead of itself, or torn, whether it be fowl or beast.

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the section against the older code throughout: shaving was forbidden outright while long hair was condemned only by implication; the prophet drops the Levitical distinction between the ordinary priest and the high priest and never mentions a high priest at all, laying down one rule falling between the two older ones; the defilement rules repeat the old law with the addition of a second seven days and a sin offering; and the carrion prohibition bound every Israelite, so no priestly peculiarity needs explaining.

Gill takes the clauses into an evangelical idiom, making the difference between holy and profane one of doctrine rather than ceremony and the controversies matter for the church rather than a court of the men of the world; he limits the wine prohibition to excess, gives practical and spiritual reasons for the mourning restriction, and reports without resolving the Jewish doctors' puzzle over the carrion rule.

Clarke supplies comparative and contemporary matter: the shaven priests of an Egyptian cult and the tenth-day shaving of an Eastern priesthood, the defiling touch of the dead among a people still living, and an extended complaint that churches professing to copy the Jewish order have dropped the clause about the priests' maintenance. Wesley ties the wine prohibition to the duty and extends it to strong drink, supplies the vanity the hair rule guards against, and states the doubled cleansing as a matter of administration.

debates.question: How far is wine forbidden to the priests?

positions.position: Whenever they go in to minister, and the ban extends to any strong drink.
Only excess is forbidden; wine is not denied to ministers for health's sake if taken in moderation, sobriety being a standing qualification.

debates.question: Why is the prohibition on eating what died of itself addressed to the priests?

positions.position: The Jewish doctors could not account for it and said Elijah would explain the verse.
There is no difficulty: the same law bound every Israelite, who threw such meat to the dogs in the wilderness and afterwards might give or sell it to a foreigner.

debates.question: What lies behind the rule about the priests' hair?

positions.position: A contrast with foreign practice, the shaven priests of an Egyptian cult and a modern clergy from whom faithful ministers must differ.
The older law, which forbade shaving outright and condemned long hair only by implication, since it allowed it in the case of a vow.
Vanity, instanced by a prince who prided himself on his hair; the polling means keeping it moderate.

outliers.claim: Observes that this prophet does not keep the older law's distinction between the ordinary priest and the high priest in marriage and mourning, and never mentions a high priest anywhere, laying down a single rule for all priests which falls between the two older ones.

Complains that churches professing to model their order on the Jewish one have all dropped this clause, living not on free offerings but on revenues secured by law, and proposes instead a portion of land for each minister or maintenance by the state as for its other officers.
